title: Elena's Knee: Recognizing Post-Traumatic Osteoarthritis in a Young Athlete
learning_goal: Learners will be able to follow a structured nursing assessment process for a young patient presenting with knee pain, correctly identifying subjective and objective data, recognizing key anatomical findings such as crepitus and reduced range of motion, and communicating findings and patient education accurately.
target_audience: High school students in nursing assistant programs and early healthcare learners
visual_style: 2D semi-flat limited animation with dynamic but constrained movement. Characters express emotion through head turns, nods, hand gestures, subtle posture shifts, and facial expressions. Mouth movement suggests speech without matching every phoneme. Consistent color palette and character designs across all clips.

Jordan enters the exam room and meets Elena, who expresses concern about ongoing right knee pain. Elena mentions she has always been active and this does not feel like a normal ache. The scene establishes the chief complaint and sets up the first decision point about what to do first.

decision_points.question_text: Elena has shared her chief complaint. What should Jordan do first?

choices.text: Pull the chair close and begin asking Elena to describe her knee pain in her own words, gathering her subjective account before touching or examining anything.
Take Elena's vital signs and move directly into the physical exam, since objective findings will be most useful for the provider.
choices.misconception: Learners may believe that measurable, objective data should always come first. In practice, the health history interview gathers essential subjective context that guides the physical exam and prevents important details from being missed.

choices.text: Reassure Elena that it is probably nothing serious at her age and suggest scheduling an X-ray right away.
choices.misconception: Learners may assume that a young, active patient is unlikely to have a significant condition. This skips the assessment process entirely and risks drawing a conclusion before any data has been gathered.

decision_points.question_text: Jordan has completed the PQRSTU pain assessment. What should Jordan ask about next before moving to the physical exam?

choices.text: Screen for the hallmark musculoskeletal symptoms such as swelling, redness, and warmth, and ask directly whether Elena has had any past injuries to this knee.
Move straight to the physical exam, since the pain assessment already covered the important details.
choices.misconception: Learners may assume that the PQRSTU assessment is sufficient on its own. Completing a full symptom screen and past injury history is still needed, as key risk factors like a prior ACL injury can be missed otherwise.

choices.text: Focus the next questions entirely on Elena's ibuprofen use, since medication safety is the most pressing concern at this point.
choices.misconception: Learners may prioritize medication safety, which is genuinely important, but isolating that single topic skips the full symptom screen and past injury history that are needed to build a complete clinical picture.

decision_points.question_text: Jordan has completed the physical exam and found mild swelling, crepitus, reduced range of motion, and mild quad weakness, with no redness, warmth, or fever. What should Jordan do with these findings?

choices.text: Document the objective findings clearly and prepare a concise report for the provider, noting what was present and confirming that there were no signs of infection or systemic inflammation.
Escalate immediately for an urgent evaluation, since swelling and grinding in the joint could indicate a joint infection.
choices.misconception: Learners may over-attribute swelling and crepitus to infection without checking for the hallmark signs. A joint infection typically presents with significant redness, heat, and often fever, none of which are present here.

choices.text: Tell Elena that the exam looks normal and there is nothing to worry about, since the findings are not dramatic.
choices.misconception: Learners may underestimate findings that are not severe or visually obvious. Swelling, crepitus, reduced range of motion, and asymmetric strength are all clinically significant and must be documented and reported accurately.

decision_points.question_text: Elena has just been told her diagnosis and is asking Jordan directly whether she will need surgery and whether she has to give up soccer. How should Jordan respond?

choices.text: Explain in plain language what osteoarthritis means, let Elena know that most cases are managed with conservative steps first, and be honest that surgery is usually considered only if those steps are not enough.
Tell Elena not to worry and that she will be totally fine, without offering any further explanation.
choices.misconception: Learners may think reassurance is more supportive than explanation. False reassurance without real information does not help the patient understand her condition or prepare for what comes next, and may increase anxiety later.

choices.text: Tell Elena those questions are for the provider and change the subject to avoid overstepping.
choices.misconception: Learners may believe that any patient education belongs solely to the provider. Offering basic plain-language explanation and emotional support in this moment is within the nursing role and is an important part of therapeutic communication.
